title: Likelihood: Likely and Unlikely
seo_title: Kindergarten Likelihood Worksheets: Free Math with Pictures and Answers (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Likelihood of familiar life events, using comparative language: using comparative language to describe likelihood (e.g., more likely, less likely, likely, unlikely)
meta_desc: Free Kindergarten math worksheets on likelihood for the BC curriculum: likely and unlikely events, which is more likely, picking from a bag, spinners and stories. 100 picture questions with answers.
key_big: Likely means it happens a lot. Unlikely means it hardly ever happens.
key_sub: More counters or more parts of a colour make it more likely.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Likely means it happens a lot. Rain in Vancouver in November is likely.
  • Unlikely means it hardly ever happens, but it still can. Seeing a whale from the beach is unlikely.
  • In a bag, the colour with more counters is more likely to be picked.
  • On a spinner, the colour with more parts is more likely.

Examples

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do
Choosing what you want to happenLook at what is there. Wanting does not change it.
Thinking fewer counters is more likelyMore counters of a colour means more likely.
Thinking unlikely means neverUnlikely things can still happen, just not often.

faq.q: What does likelihood mean in Kindergarten?
faq.a: Talking about how likely familiar events are, using words such as likely, unlikely, more likely and less likely.

faq.q: What is the difference between unlikely and never?
faq.a: Unlikely things hardly ever happen but still can. Never means it cannot happen at all.

faq.q: How can I practise at home?
faq.a: Put 6 red and 2 blue blocks in a bag and pick without looking. Talk about which colour you get more often.
Children already know about rain, school days and birthdays, so they can judge what happens a lot and what hardly ever happens.
